answer:
**Final data-grounded hypothesis (answering the question):**

The effect of increasing education expenditure (% of GNI) on per-capita economic output is **statistically indistinguishable between Sub-Saharan Africa and developing (lower-middle-income) countries**. Using exports growth as the economic-output proxy — the only outcome statistically comparable across both groups, given that SSA's GNI per capita exists for only 2011–2015 — the estimated long-run effect of a one-percentage-point rise in education expenditure is **+4.7 percentage points for SSA (95% CI 0.4 to 8.9)** and **+6.0 percentage points for developing countries (95% CI −1.3 to 13.2)**, a between-group difference of only **+1.3 pp that is clearly insignificant (Wald p = 0.77)**. Both point estimates are positive but imprecise and economically implausible in magnitude, and the direct GNI per-capita-growth evidence is inconsistent (negative, largely insignificant point estimates for LMC; unestimable for SSA at n=4 growth observations). Therefore the data do not establish a robustly positive or materially different effect of education spending on per-capita economic output between the two groups.

**Why (evidence summary).** Primary comparative model (approved plan): per-group ARDL(1,1) on exports growth (common 1991–2015 window, Newey–West HAC) — SSA long-run multiplier LR=+4.68 (se 2.17, CI [0.43, 8.94], persistence ρ=0.11); LMC LR=+5.96 (se 3.72, CI [−1.33, 13.24], ρ=0.12). Stacked interaction Wald test of LR equality: difference LMC−SSA = +1.27 (se 4.37), z=0.29, **p=0.771**. Robustness: (i) lag-only variant (no contemporaneous edu): SSA +6.76 (CI [2.12, 11.41], sig), LMC +1.70 (CI ns), difference p=0.40 — still no significant group difference, SSA's positive effect robust; (ii) with labor-force control the SSA LR flips to −1.71 (ns, wide CI) — a sensitivity flag, but that spec is unstable because LF participation is near-constant; (iii) enrollment outcomes are near-unit-root (ρ≈0.96–1.01), making their long-run multipliers non-identifiable and short-run education effects mostly insignificant — no robust human-capital-accumulation effect. Direct GNI growth: LMC full-sample LR −3.08 (se 3.66, CI [−10.3, 4.1], ns); LMC matched-window (fragile) LR −2.30 (se 1.05, CI [−4.4, −0.2], sig-neg); SSA descriptive only — 4 growth observations (2012–2015), mean +1.24%/yr, corr(edu, GNI growth) −0.56, **no cross-group test possible on that variable**. Proxy validity: corr(exports growth, GNI per-capita growth) = 0.74 (LMC full), 0.48 (LMC 1991–2015), 0.94 (SSA, n=4).

Both point estimates are positive but imprecise/implausibly large, and the direct GNI per-capita-growth evidence is inconsistent (negative, largely insignificant for LMC; unestimable for SSA at n=4), so no robustly positive or materially different effect is established.
payload.workflow: Wides CSV → long panel (2 groups × 41 years, 6 indicators). ARDL(1,1) with Newey-West HAC per group on the exports-growth proxy (common 1991-2015 window); long-run multiplier=(beta+delta)/(1-rho) with delta-method CI; stacked interaction model with nonlinear Wald test of LR equality. Robustness: lag-only variant, labor-force control, enrollments as intermediate outcomes, window-matched LMC; direct GNI per-capita growth for LMC (full and matched windows) and descriptive-only for SSA (2011-2015, n=4). Proxy validity check: corr(exports growth, GNI per-capita growth)=0.74 (LMC full).
